rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~79% (from 71% a week ago); ECB Dec ~89% (Nov 4); BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~35%; RBNZ Dec <50%; BoE 4.00% and RBA 4.85% after November hikes
rows.read: A December Federal Reserve hike stays the market's main expectation after last week's strong US jobs report, which keeps rate support under the dollar. Hikes are also expected in Europe and Japan, while job losses in Canada and New Zealand give those banks reasons to wait. Tuesday's US inflation figures are the next big check.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US payrolls +165K (fcst 65K), unemployment 4.1%; Canada −4.7K, unemployment 6.7%; NZ unemployment 5.7%; China Oct CPI 0.7% y/y (fcst 0.8%); UK Q3 GDP Thu 1:00 AM CT, fcst +0.7% q/q
rows.read: The US job market looks much firmer than Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the US dollar. China's figures showed weak shopping at home, a soft spot for the currencies that sell to it, like the Aussie and the kiwi. UK growth figures on Thursday are the next big read.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: China PPI 5.7% y/y (fcst 5.3%, four-year high); US Sep CPI 3.7% y/y, Oct due Tue 7:30 AM CT (fcst +0.3% m/m, core +0.2%); euro-area Oct 4.0%; Brent ~$98
rows.read: Factory prices in China are climbing fast on dear oil while shop prices cool, so the energy shock is still working through supply chains. US inflation is well above the Fed's goal, and Tuesday's figures will show whether it is cooling. Hot prices would favour the dollar; soft ones would weigh on it.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Nikkei +3.45%, Taiex +5.72%, Kospi +1.68% (04:00 GMT Mon); S&P 500 futures +0.6%; Friday: Nikkei ~−6%, Kospi ~−9%
rows.read: Asian stocks bounced hard after last week's AI and chip-stock rout, so fear eased and demand for safe havens faded a little. The Aussie and the kiwi, which were hit hardest, won back some ground. News that Nvidia's board is investigating its chief executive barely dented the mood.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$98.32 (flat), WTI ~$91.31; Brent $116.72 at the Oct 30 close; Khor Mor gas field halted (local power, not exports)
rows.read: Oil held near $98 a barrel as softer US war talk and fresh attacks around the Gulf cancelled each other out. Prices well below October's highs ease the bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. They also give less support to the Canadian dollar.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Nov 3: hedge funds for USD, JPY, AUD, GBP; against NZD (19th percentile), CAD (21st), EUR (35th); 4-week change NZD −22K, EUR −34K contracts; real money very bearish GBP and AUD
rows.read: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and over the past month they sharply added to their bets against the kiwi and the euro. In the Aussie and the pound, hedge funds and real-money investors sit on opposite sides, with real money betting heavily against both.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: NZ governing bloc 67 of 131 seats, official result Nov 27; Democrats control House and Senate; Canada deficits C$50–60B a year ahead; France on negative outlook at Moody's
rows.read: No new budget news moved currencies overnight. New Zealand's election count points to the same coalition staying, which lowers the risk of a big budget change. A Democratic Congress still makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar.
